property_summary: For every caller context, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the initializer-set _owner), whereas the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ from the stored owner for many callers and thus breaks this invariant for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For every caller context, the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the initializer-set owner) while the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ when calls are made via an intermediate contract — so for all inputs the reference returns the same owner when invoked through any caller, but the mutant can return a different address when invoked through a contract caller (whose tx.origin differs).

For any caller (EOA or contract), the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the same value no matter who calls); the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ when called through an intermediate contract, so there exists a caller contract address that makes owner() return a different value in the mutant but not in the reference.

For every caller (EOA or contract), C.owner() returns the stored owner address (the initializer-set _owner); the mutant returns tx.origin instead, so when called via a contract (where tx.origin is the original EOA), the mutant can return a different address while the reference always returns the stored owner.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored owner address initialized by initialize(), while the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ when the call originates from a contract; thus owner() should be invariant under caller identity (the returned owner equals the stored owner) for all callers — the mutant violates this for some contract callers.

For any non-zero address newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership must succeed on the reference; the mutant that removes the non-zero check will also succeed for non-zero but additionally allows transferring to address(0) — we assert that transferOwnership reverts when newOwner == address(0) (reference reverts for that input, mutant does not).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert if newOwner is the zero address (reference enforces non-zero newOwner); the mutant removes that check and thus will allow transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed for some fuzzed inputs.

For all callers that are the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert when newOwner == address(0); the mutant removed that check so it will sometimes succeed (violating the rule) for newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with the zero address must revert (reference enforces non-zero newOwner); the mutant removed that check and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed for some inputs, violating the rule.

For every caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) MUST revert when newOwner == address(0); the mutant removes that require and therefore allows the call to succeed for some inputs (violating this rule).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (i.e., does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant forbids changing to any newOwner != current owner causing calls with a different newOwner to revert or leave owner unchanged.

For any caller who is the current owner and any fuzzed address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds on the reference and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant erroneously forbids changing owner when newOwner != current owner, causing transferOwnership to revert (or leave owner unchanged) for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any caller who is the current owner and any fuzzed address newOwner, the reference contract always allows transferOwnership(newOwner) to succeed (owner() becomes newOwner); the mutant erroneously requires newOwner == current owner, so for many fuzzed newOwner values the call will revert (or fail to change owner).

For any caller that is the current owner and any target address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract succeeds (call does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant wrongly requires newOwner == current owner, so some fuzzed newOwner values will make transferOwnership revert or fail to change owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any fuzzed address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract succeeds and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant forbids changing owner to any different address (requires newOwner == current owner) so some fuzzed newOwner values will cause the call to revert or leave owner unchanged.

For any caller address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner succeeds (does not revert) and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant blocks calls when the stored owner is the zero address by requiring owner() != address(0), causing transferOwnership to revert when ownership was previously renounced (owner == address(0)).

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner always succeeds (does not revert) and updates owner() to newOwner for every admissible newOwner; the mutant can revert when the stored owner is address(0) (after renounceOwnership) because it additionally requires owner() != address(0), so calls that should succeed on the reference (even after renounce on reference the owner() becomes zero and transferOwnership from zero is impossible but on reference transferOwnership called by the zero address is allowed only via initializer rules—the concrete distinguishing behavior is that after renounceOwnership() followed by transferOwnership(newOwner) invoked via the contract's current owner behavior differs: the reference allows transferOwnership to set owner to newOwner when called by the previous owner (including when owner() == address(0) the reference's check compares equal and only checks msg.sender equality), while the mutant blocks when owner() == address(0)).

For any caller address newOwner and any actor caller, if transferOwnership(newOwner) is invoked by the current owner (msg.sender == owner()), the call should succeed (not revert) and owner() should become newOwner; the mutant adds a check that owner() != address(0) and thus can revert when the stored owner is address(0) even if msg.sender == owner(), violating this rule for inputs where owner() == address(0).

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should succeed (not revert) and set owner() to newOwner; the mutant adds owner() != address(0) which causes transferOwnership to revert when the stored owner is address(0), violating this rule for those inputs.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant additionally requires stored owner != address(0) and thus can revert when the stored owner is zero, violating this rule for inputs where owner() == address(0).

For every input, the reference contract returns paused() == _paused (i.e., paused() reflects the internal paused flag); the mutant inverts this so paused() returns the opposite, breaking that relation for some inputs.

For every input the reference contract's paused() return equals the internal _paused flag (so paused() flips when _pause/_unpause change it); the mutant inverts paused()'s return, so there exists an input where paused()'s return differs from the real internal paused state (observable via calling pause/unpause behavior), which the test detects by toggling pause state via keeper/owner flows and checking paused() vs expected.

For every sequence of owner/keeper actions, the public paused() view must report the actual paused state of the contract (true after _pause, false after _unpause); the mutant inverts that return causing paused() to disagree with the real paused state for some sequences.

The public paused() view must accurately report the contract's actual pause state after calling pause/unpause flows (i.e., paused() == true right after a keeper pauses and == false right after keeper unpauses); the mutant inverts the returned value causing a mismatch for some inputs.

The reference contract's public paused() view reports the actual internal pause state (_paused) for every sequence of pause/unpause actions; the mutant inverts paused() so there exists a sequence (pause then unpause or vice versa) where paused()'s return differs from the real state, which the test detects by calling pause/unpause and checking paused() matches the expected boolean.

Invariant: calling setKeeper with any address should succeed (not revert) and set c.keeper() to the supplied address; the mutant disallows setting the zero address (reverts), so there exist inputs (address(0)) where the mutant breaks this rule.

For any address x passed to setKeeper by the owner, the reference contract always updates keeper to x (call succeeds and keeper()==x); the mutant rejects the zero address and thus for x == address(0) the call reverts (keeper not updated).

For any address newKeeper supplied by the owner, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) succeeds and updates c.keeper() to newKeeper in the reference; the mutant rejects the zero address causing the call to revert and not update keeper.

For any caller who is the owner, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) on the reference always succeeds (does not revert) and results in keeper() equaling newKeeper; the mutant prevents setting keeper to the zero address (reverting), so there exists an input (newKeeper == address(0)) where the mutant fails this property.

For any address newKeeper supplied by the owner, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) on the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) and results in keeper() equaling newKeeper; the mutant adds a require disallowing the zero address, so when newKeeper == address(0) the mutant reverts and keeper() is not updated.
